司法院大法官會台字第12 6 4號鑑定意見發言要點
李念祖
一 、關於破除性別歧視 （ 憲法增修條文第10條第 6 項）

> 釋 字第748號解釋出現後必須重新檢視刑法的配偶定義與釋
字 第 554號 解 釋 。
> 婚姻制度的演變，已從過去不平等的身分性別關係轉變為現
代性別平等的契約關係。
> 配偶的不通姦義務， 是契約當事人的原生義務， 不是親族間
的出嫁從夫義務； 第三人的不相姦義務， 則是婚姻登記後的
法律衍生義務， 兩者之性質不同。民法未能明示兩項義務，
只能透過其他條文意會， 不無闕憾。
> 用刑法懲處通姦與相姦行為， 是傳統禮教人倫秩序， 強制建
立男尊女卑身分關係，出禮入刑的思想遺留； 刑法雖採看似
性別中立的法條文字， 仍對男尊女卑的社會刻板意識欠缺免
疫 力 。配偶可選擇處罰同性相姦者而宥恕異性配偶的告訴乃
論制度(刑法第2 3 9條以及刑訴第2 3 9條但書，有使刑罰公權
力成為配偶復仇的工具， 並且繼續復刻並延長鞏固男尊女卑、
不平等的身分性別關係之虞。
• 印度 Dipak Misra 大法官在 2018 年 Joseph Shine V . Union of
India — 案判決開篇之處即云：「 任何制度歧視女性， 或侵
犯女性尊嚴、 公允與平等原則者， 都足以在憲法上引起憤
慨 ； 以致於逝者如斯而不舍晝夜， 即使過去數十年間曾有
任何相關法令條文得到沈默的支持背書， 隨著日趨成熟的

立法的正當性。 最緊要的是女性的收入及經濟能力因社會

women . Women were socialy and economicaly underprivileged , and
acts of adultery were mainly comited by men . Therefore , thexistence of an adultery crime acted as psychological deterence for
men , and , furthermore , enabled female spouses to receive payment of
compensation for grief or divided asets from the male spouse on the
condition of canceling the adultery acusation . However , the changes
of our society diluted the justification of criminal punishment of
adultery . Above al , as women’s earning power and economicapabilities have improved with more active social and economic
activities , the premise that women are theconomicaly disadvantagedoes not aply to al maried couples . )
> 歷年相關刑事資料統計數字足以證明， 傳統上男尊女卑之社
會刻板意識仍然存在而且緣附於刑法第2 3 9及刑訴2 3 9但書
作 用 ， 延續了通姦關係中男性受到宥恕而女性不受宥恕的優
越 地 位 ； 婚姻的性別平等契約關係， 也因之回到了不平等的
身分性別關係。

普遍體認自身負有消除性別歧視， 促進性別平等的憲法義務

二 、關於比例原則
> 較小之侵害手段， 至 少 有 二 ， 一是於 民法中明確載入 ， 有配
> 二是 只罰配偶， 以避免性別歧視 。 但大法官必須補充釋748

與 職 責 （ 憲法增修條文第10條 第 6 項 ） 。 大院為憲法機關，
負有相同的憲法義務。 釋 字第 3 72號即為使用此條項之一項
前 例 。
> 本案系爭法律限制基本人權 （ 包括憲法第22條所保障者， 無
論以隱私權， 或如釋字第554號以性自主自由稱之皆無不可） ，
涉及實際性別歧視 （ 釋 字第 6 號 ）與限制人身自由的刑罰
規 定 ， 應依比例原則施以嚴格審查。
> 系爭規定表面上在防止通姦以維繫婚姻， 卻在實質配合配偶
復仇並延續也助長男尊女卑之社會刻板意識， 即不能認為具
有特別重要之公共利益。
> 刑罰追訴能否直接而實質地達到預防通姦與維繫婚姻的實際
效 用 ， 不能徒憑假設。沒有實證資料顯示獲得宥恕配偶之再
犯率及其婚姻之維持率如何，即無從證明其手段必要性果然
存 在 。
偶者不得通姦， 以及第三人不得與他人之配偶為性行為兩項
義 務 ， 並提高賠償額度與慰撫金， 以替代刑罰， 也可避免除
罪化引起通姦具有社會相當性的誤會，同時消除國庫與民事
原告自被告之財產求償發生任何競爭關係。
解 釋 ， 說明配偶的定義是否不因性傾向而有差異。
> 以上二者均指向系爭規定不符限制妥當性而屬違憲立法的結

論 。
> 至於主張民事賠償是給予富人以金錢換取不法的說法， 至少
有兩個錯誤。
1 . 此一論據如果成立， 民法賠償責任制度， 豈不盡在獎勵富
人為侵權行為而悉應改以刑罰施之？民事法院原得斟酌
富人被告之財力而判給與其財力相當之賠償， 此則與刑罰
秩序無涉。問題不只在於損害賠償並不等於用金錢換取違
法 行 為 ， 也在違約的公平法律救濟， 並不依賴施以刑罰嚇
阻 補 充 。
2 . 在婚姻私事上也迷信刑罰萬能而不重民事救濟， 正是國家
秩序無遠弗屆，出禮入刑， 刑罰直入家門以貫徹人倫秩序
的德治傳統思想路徑。而通姦成罪， 以刑替民甚或以刑逼
民 ， 是民事救濟欠發達的舊時法律文化特徵， 也是婚姻制
度 ， 從身分轉變到契約迄今猶是困難重， 無法擺脫禮教
社會中男性配偶的優越地位， 也難以破除社會性別刻板意
識的重大障礙。

ofence is comited by both of them , one is
liable for the criminal ofence buthe other

societal presumption . Ordinarily , the
criminalaw proceds on gender neutrality
but in this provision , as we perceive , the

sen when there is conferment of any
afirmative right on women , can it go to thextent of treating them as the victim , in al
circumstances , to the peril of the husband .

the languagemployed in the Section thathe fulcrum of the ofence is destroyed once
the consent or the conivance of the
husband is established . Viewed from the
said scenario , the provision realy creates a
dent on the individual independent identity
of a woman when themphasis laid on
the conivance or the consent of the
husband . This tantamounts to

a woman is equal to a man in every field .

quite archaic . When the society progres
and the rights are confered , the new
generation of thoughtspring , and that is
why , we are inclined to isue notice . ”
That is how the mater has ben placed before us .

55. In this regard, another aspect deserves to be noted. The
jurisprudence in England, which to a largextent, is adopted by
this country has neveregarded adultery as a crimexcept for a
period of ten years in the reign of Puritanical Oliver Cromwel. As

Articles 14 a n d 21 of the Constitution. Thinking of adultery from
the point of view of criminality would be a retrograde step. This
Court has traveled on the path of transformative
constitutionalism and, therefore, it is absolutely inapropriate to
sit in a time machine to a diferent era where the machine m o v e s
o n the path of regresion. Hence, to treat adultery as a crime
would be unwaranted in law.

Causes Act, 18 57 abolished the comon law action for criminal
conversation while retaing, by Section XI of the same Act,
the power to award the husbandamages for adultery
comited by the wife. This position continued rightil 192 3,
when the Matrimonial Causes Act, 192 3 made adultery a
ground for divorce available to both spouses instead of only the
husband. The right of a husband to claim damages for adultery
was abolished very recently by the Law Reforms
(Miscelaneous Provisions) Act, 1 9 7 0 . 1 6
8 . In the United States, however, Puritans who wento make
a living in the American colonies, caried withem Cromwel’s
criminalaw, thereby making adultery a capital ofence.
Strangely enough, thistil continues in some of the States in
the United States. The American Law Institute, however, has
droped the crime of adultery from its Model Penal Code as
adultery statutes are in general vague, archaic, and sexist.

any modern Code of law. Days are past, we hope,
when women were loked upon as property by their
husbands. Buthat is an argument more in favour of
doing away with Section 49 7 altogether.” 2 0

nations retain adultery for the purposes of divorce laws. Thus,
adultery continues to be a criminal ofence in Afghanistan,
Bangladesh, Indonesia, Iran, Maldives, Nepal, Pakistan,
Philipines, United Arab Emirates, some states of the United
States of America, Algeria, Democratic Republic of Congo,
Egypt, Moroco, and some parts of Nigeria.
On the other hand, a number of jurisdictions have done away
with adultery as a crime. The People’s Republic of China,
Japan, Brazil, New Zealand, Australia, Scotland, the
Netherlands, Denmark, France, Germany, Austria, the Republic
of Ireland, Barbados, Bermuda, Jamaica, Trinidad and Tobago,
Seycheles etc. are some of the jurisdictions in which it has
ben done away with. In South Korea 2 1 and Guatemala, 2
provisionsimilar to Section 49 7 have ben struck down by the
constitutional courts of those nations.

and liberties. It envisages the creation of a society w here the ideals of equality,
dignity and fredom triumph over entrenched prejudices and injustices. The
creation of a just, egalitarian society is a proces. It often involves the
questioning and obliteration of parochial social m ores which are antithetical to
constitutional morality. The case at hand enjoins this constitutional courto m ake
an enquiry into the insidious perm eation of patriarchal values into the legal order
and its role in perpetuatingender injustices.
2 Law and society are intrinsicaly conected and opresive social values

societal values are slow to adapto leadshown by the law. The law on adultery
canot be construed in isolation. To fuly com prehend its nature and impact,
every legislative provision must be understod as a ‘discourse’ about social
structuring. 1 However, the discourse of law is not hom ogenous.2 In the context
particularly of Section 497, it regards individuals as ‘gendered citizens’.3 In doing
so, the law creates and ascribes genderoles based on existing societal

Section 497 reads thus:
“ Whoever hasexual intercourse with a person who is and

another man, withouthe consent or conivance of that man,

imprisonment of either description for a term which may
extend to five years, or with fine, or with both. In such case

the husband, some person who had care of the woman on his

pages.text:
PART B
Article 228. The High Court decided againsthe apelant 10 , but Chief Justice
Chagla m ade an observation abouthe asumption underlying Section 497:
“ Mr Perbhoy is right when he says thathe underlying idea
of Section 49 7 is that wives are properties of their husbands.
The very facthathe ofence is only cognizable withe
consent of the husband emphasises that point of view. It may
be argued that Section 49 7 should not find a place in any
modern Code of law. Days are past, when women were
loked upon as property by their husbands.”
A narow chalenge w as adresed before this Court. The judgm ent of Justice
Vivian Bose records the nature of the chalenge:
“ 3. Under Section 49 7 the ofence of adultery can only be
comited by a man but in the absence of any provision to
the contrary the woman would be punishable as an abetor.
The last sentence in Section 49 7 prohibits this. It runs—
“ In such case the wife shal not be punishable as an abetor^5.
It isaid thathis ofends Articles 14 and 1 5.”
Hence, the chalenge w as only to the prohibition treating the wife as an
abetor. It w as this chalenge which w as dealt with and repeled on the ground
that Article 1 4 must be read withe other provisions of Part I which prescribe
the am bit of the fundam ental rights. The prohibition treating the wife as an
abetor w as upheld as a special provision which isaved by Article 1 5(3). The
conclusion w as that:
“ 5. Article 14 is general and must be read withe other
provisions which set outhe ambit ofundamental rights. Sex
is a sound clasification and although there can be no
discrimination in general on that ground, the Constitution itself
provides for special provisions in the case of women and
children. The two articles read together validate the impugned
clause in Section 49 7 of the Indian Penal Code.”
10 AIR 19 5 1 Bom 4 7 0

pages.text:
PART B
7 The chalenge was to a limited part of Section 497: that which prohibited a
wom an from being prosecuted as an abetor. Broader isuesuch as w hether (i)
the punishm ent for adultery violates Article 2 1 ; (i) the statutory provision sufers
from anifest arbitrarines; (i) the legislature has, while ostensibly protecting
the sanctity of m ariage, invaded the dignity of wom en; and (iv) Section 497
violates Article 1 5( 1 ) by enforcingender stereotypes w ere neither adresed
before this Court nor w ere they dealt with.
This Court construed thexem ption granted to wom en from criminal sanctions as
a ‘special provision' for the benefit of wom en and thus, protected under Article
1 5(3) of the Constitution. In U nion o f India v E lphinstone S ping and
W eaving Co. L td , 1 a Constitution Bench of this Court held:
“1 7 … When the question arises as to the meaning of a certain
provision in a statute it is not only legitimate but proper to
read that provision in its context. The context means the
statute as a whole, the previoustate of law, other statutes in
pari materia, the general scope of the statute and the mischief

1 2 The decision of a two judge Bench in V R evathi v U nion o f In d ia 1 7
involved a chalenge to Section 497 (read with Section 1 98(2) of the Code of
Criminal Procedure) which disables a wife from prosecuting her husband for
being involved in an adulterous relationship. The court noted that Section 497
permits neither the husband of the ofending wife to prosecute her nor does it
permithe wife to prosecute her ofending husband for being disloyal. This
formal sense of equality found aceptance by the court. The chalenge was
repeled by relying on the decision in S ow m ithri V ishnu. Observing that Section
497 and Section 1 98(2) constitute a “legislative packet”， the court observed thathe provision does not alow either the wife to prosecute an ering husband or a
husband to prosecute thering wife. In the view of the court, this indicated thathere is no discrimination the ground of sex. In the view of the court :
“ 5 … The law does not envisage the punishment of any of the
spouses athe instance of each other. Thus there is no
discrimination againsthe woman insofar ashe is not
permited to prosecute her husband. A husband is not
permited because the wife is notreated as an ofender in theye of law. The wife is not permited as Section 198 ( 1 ) read
with Section 198 ( 2 ) does not permit her to do so. In the
ultimate analysis the law has meted out even-handed justice
to both of them in the mater of prosecuting each other or
securing the incarceration of each other. Thus no
discrimination has ben practised in circumscribing the scope
of Section 198 ( 2 ) and fashioning it so thathe righto
prosecute the adulter is restricted to the husband of the
adulteres but has not ben extended to the wife of the
adulter.” 1 8

PART C
1 7 O nce m onogam y cam e to be acepted as the norm in Britain betwen the
fourth and fifth centuries, adultery cam e to be recognized as a serious wrong that
interfered with a husband's “rights” over his w ife.3 1 The imposition of criminal
sanctions on adultery was also largely based on ideas and beliefs about sexual
morality which acquired the force of law in Christian Europe during the M idle
A ges.32 The developm ent of canon law in the twelfth century enshrined the
perception of adultery as a spiritual m isdem eanour. In the sixtenth century,
folowing the Reform ation, adultery becam e a crucial isue because Protestants
placed new em phasis on m ariage as a linchpin of the social and moral order.33
Several prominent sixtenth century reformers, including Martin Luther and John
Calvin, argued that a m ariage w as ireparably dam aged by infidelity, and they
advocatedivorce in such cases.34
Concerned withe “moral coruption” prevalent in England since the
Reform ation, Puritans in the M asachusets Bay Colony introduced the death
penalty for comiting adultery.35 The strict morality of thearly English colonists
is reflected in the fam ous 1 85 0 novel ‘The Scarlet Leter' by Nathaniel

“ For the supresing of the abominable and crying sins

Almighty God highly displeased; be it enacted.That in case
any maried woman shal … be carnaly known by any man
(other than her husband) … as wel the man as the
woman … shal sufer death.”

another for unlawful copulation withis female chatel.”

and principal architect of the IPC, considered the posibility of criminalizing
adultery in India, and ultimately concluded that it would serve litle purpose.5 0
Acording to Lord M acaulay, the posible benefits from an adultery ofence could
beter achieved through pecuniary com pensation.5 1 Section 497 did not find a
place in the first Draft Penal Code prepared by Lord M acaulay. On an apraisal
of the facts and opinions colected from al thre Presidencies abouthe
feasibility criminalizing adultery, he concluded in his Notes to the IPC that:
Al thexisting laws for the punishment of adultery are
altogether ineficacious for the purpose of preventing injured
husbands of the higher clases from taking the law into their
own hands; secondly; that scarcely any native of higher
clases ever has recourse to the courts of law in a case of
adultery foredres against either his wife, or her galant;
thirdly, thathe husbands who have recourse in case of
adultery to the Courts of law are generaly por men whose
wives have run away, thathese husbandseldom have any
delicate felings abouthe intrigue, buthink themselves
injured by thelopement, thathey consider wives as useful
members of their smal households, thathey generaly
complainot of the wound given to their afections, not of the
stain on their honor , but of the los of a menial whom they
canot easily replace, and that generaly their principal object
is thathe women may be sent back.” These things being
established, it sems to us that no advantage is to bexpected from providing a punishment for adultery. We
think it besto treat adultery merely as a civil injury.”5 2
(Emphasisuplied)

disagred with Lord M acaulay’s view. Placing heavy reliance upon the status of
wom en in India, they concluded that:

PART C
“ While we think thathe ofence of adultery ought noto be
omited from the code, we would limits cognizance to
adultery comited with a maried woman, and considering
thathere is much weight in the last remark inote Q,
regarding the condition of the women, in this country, in
deference to it, we would render the male ofender alone
liable to punishment. We would, however, puthe parties
acused of adultery on trial “ together ”， and empower the
Court in thevent of their conviction to pronounce a decre of
divorce againsthe guilty woman, if the husband sues for it, athe same time that her paramour isentenced to punishment
by imprisonment or fine.”53
The Law Com isioners' decision to insert Section 497 into the IPC w as roted
in their concern abouthe posibility of the “natives” resorting to ilegal m easures
to avenge the injury in cases of adultery:

PART C
and wom en diferently is, ultimately, to act in w om en's interests.6 0 The status of
Section 497 as a “special provision”6 1 operating for the benefit of wom en,
therefore, constitutes a paradigm atic exam ple of benevolent patriarchy.
25 Throughout history, the law has failed to ask the wom an question.62 It has
failed to interogate the generalizations or stereotypes abouthe nature,
character and abilities of the sexes on which laws rest, and how these notions
afect wom en and their interaction withe law. A wom an's ‘purity’ and a m an's
marital ‘entitlem ent' to her exclusive sexual posesion m ay be reflective of the
antiquated social and sexual m ores of the ninetenth century, buthey canot be
recognized as being so today. It is nothe “com on morality” of the State at any
tim e in history, but rather constitutional morality, which must guide the law. In any
dem ocracy, constitutional morality requires the asurance of certain rights that
are indispensable for the fre, equal, andignified existence of al m em bers of
society. A com itm ento constitutional morality requires us to enforce the
constitutional guarantes of equality before law, non-discrimination acount of
sex, andignity, al of which are afected by the operation of Section 497.

PART D
26 The last few decades have ben characterized by num erous countries
around the world taking m easures to decrim inalize the ofence of adultery due to
the gender discriminatory nature of adultery laws as wel as on the ground thathey violate the righto privacy. However, progresive action has primarily ben
taken on the ground that provisions penalising adultery are discriminatory against
wom en either patently on the face of the law or in their implem entation. Reform
towards achieving a m oregalitarian society in practice has also ben driven by
active m easures taken by the United Nations and other international human
rights organizations, w here it has ben em phasized that even sem ingly gender-
neutral provisions criminalising adultery cast an unequal burden on w om en:63
“ Given continuediscrimination and inequalities faced by
women, including inferioroles atributed to them by
patriarchal and traditional atitudes, and power imbalances in
theirelations with men, the mere fact of maintaing adultery
as a criminal ofence, even when it aplies to both women
and men, means in practice that women mainly wil continue
to facextreme vulnerabilities, and violation of their human
rights to dignity, privacy and equality.”
The abolishing of adultery has ben brought about in equal m easure by
legislatures and courts. W hen decisions have ben handedown by the judiciary
acros the world, it has led to the creation of a rich body of transnational
jurisprudence. Thisection wil focus on a few select com parative decisions
em anating from the courts of those countries w here the provision criminalizing
adultery has ben struck down through judicial action. The decisions of these

27 In 2 0 1 5, the South Korean Constitutional Court,64 by a majority of 7-2
struck down Article 24 1 of the Criminal Law; a provision which criminalized
adultery with a term of imprisonment of two years as unconstitutional. In doing
so, South Korea joined a growing list of countries in Asiand inded around the
world that have taken the m easure of efacing the ofence of adultery from the
statute boks, considering evolving public values and societal trends. The
Constitutional Court hadeliberated upon the legality of the provision four tim es
previously65, but chose to strike it down when it cam e before it in 2 0 1 5, withe
Court's judgem ent acknowledging the shifting public perception of individual
rights in their private lives.

PART D
Next, the Court analysed the apropriatenes and efectivenes of criminal
punishm ent in curbing the ofence of adultery. Adresing the question of
w hether adultery should be regulated, the Court stated that modern criminalaw
dictated thathe State should not sek to interfere in an acthat is not socialy
harmful or deleterious to legal interests, simply because it is repugnanto
morality. M oreover, it held thathe State had no busines in seking to control
an individual’s actions which w ere within the sphere of his or her constitutionaly
protected rights of privacy and self-determ ination.
Moving on to thefectivenes of the provision at hand, the Court rem arked that
criminalizing adultery did not help save a failing m ariage. The Court rem arked
that it w as obvious that once a spouse w as acused of adultery, the
consequence w as generaly intensified spousal conflict as oposed to the
posibility ofam ily harm ony:
“ Existing families face breakdown withe invoking of the
righto file an acusation. Even after cancelation of the
acusation, it is dificulto hope for emotional recovery
betwen spouses. Therefore, the adultery crime cano
longer contribute to protecting the marital system or family
order. Furthermore, there is litle posibility that a person who
was punished for adultery would remary the spouse who had
made an acusation against himself/herself. It is neither
posible to protect harmonious family order because of the
intensified conflict betwen spouses in the proces of criminal
punishment of adultery.”6 9

sexual self-determination and the changed recognition
sex, despite of the punishment of adultery. Acordingly, it is

al maried couples.”

PART D
The Respondent prayed thathe Court consider making the provision of adultery
equal in its treatm ent of men and wom en, instead of striking it down completely.
However, in its holding, the Court denied this request, holding it could not
prescribe a punishm ent under penalaw to change the statute. The Court held
that Section 1 54 of the Penal Code w as wholy unconstitutional as being violative
of the provisions of the Constitution, and rem arked:
“… the respondent did not point outo us areas that his Court
can or should modify and adapto bring them in conformity
withe provisions of the Constitution. The section is a penal
one and this Court in our considered opinion canot create a
sentence thathe courts can impose on adulterouspouses.
Consequently, it is our finding thathe provision of section
1 5 4 of the Penal Code Act is inconsistent withe stated
provisions of the Constitution and it is void.”75 7 6

PART E
cabined and confined” within traditional andoctrinaire
limits. From a positivistic point of view, equality is
antithetic to arbitrarines. In fact equality and
arbitrarines are sworn enemies; one belongs to the rule
of law in a republic while the other, to the whim and
caprice of an absolute monarch. Where an act is
arbitrary, it is implicit in ithat it is unequal both
acording to politicalogic and constitutionalaw and is
therefore violative of Article 14 … ” 1 0 1
(Emphasisuplied)
The Constitution Bench in S hayara B ano v U nion o f In d ia 10 2 held the practice of
Triple Talaq to be unconstitutional. Justice Rohinton Narim an, in his concuring
opinion, aplied the test of m anifest arbitrarines to hold thathe practice does
not pas constitutional muster:
“8 7. The thread of reasonablenes runs through thentire fundamental rights chapter. What is manifestly
arbitrary is obviously unreasonable and being contrary to
the rule of law, would violate Article 14 . Further, there is an
aparent contradiction in the thre-Judge Bench decision
in McDowel [State of A.P. v. McDowel and Co., ( 199 6) 3
SC 7 09 ] when it isaid that a constitutional chalenge can
suced on the ground that a law is “ disproportionate,
excesive or unreasonable”， yet suchalenge would fail on
the very ground of the law being “ unreasonable, unecesary
or unwaranted”. The arbitrarines doctrine when aplied to
legislation obviously would not involve the later chalenge but
would only involve a law being disproportionate, excesive or
otherwise being manifestly unreasonable. Al the aforesaid
grounds, therefore, do not sek to diferentiate betwen State
action in its various forms, al of which are interdicted if they
fal foul of the fundamental rights guaranted to persons and
citizens in Part I of the Constitution.” 1 0 3

legislation as wel asubordinate legislation under Article 14 .

adequate determing principle. Also, when something is

negate legislation as wel under Article 14 .” 1 0 4

PART G
“ In order to understand how sexual choices are an esential
atribute of autonomy, it is useful to refer to John Rawls5
theory on social contract. Rawls’ conception of the ‘Original
Position’ serves as a constructive model to ilustrate the
notion of choice behind a “ partial veil of ignorance.” Persons
behind the veil are asumed to be rational and mutualy
disinterested individuals, unaware of their positions in society.
The strategy employed by Rawls is to focus on a category of
gods which an individual wouldesirespective of what
individuals’ conception of ‘god’ might be. These neutraly
desirable gods are described by Rawls as ‘primary social
gods’ and may be listed as rights, liberties, powers,
oportunities, income, wealth, and the constituents of self­
respect. Rawls's conception of self-respect, as a primary
human god, is intimately conected to the idea of
autonomy. Self-respect is founded on an individual's
ability to exercise her native capacities in a competent
maner.”
(Emphasisuplied)
